analysis.one_liner: Replaces private health insurance with a government plan covering everyone, with no deductibles or copays.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the two years before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a national health insurance program run by the Department of Health and Human Services covering every U.S. resident automatically, including hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health care, dental and vision, home-based long-term care, and reproductive care. It would ban deductibles, copays, and coinsurance for covered care (with a small annual cap on drug charges), end the ACA marketplaces, and make it illegal for private insurers or employers to sell or provide coverage that duplicates the government plan. The program would phase in over four years, with children covered first and a temporary Medicare buy-in for older adults.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident, especially the roughly 26 million uninsured and the tens of millions more who skip or delay care because of deductibles, copays, or lack of dental, vision, or long-term care coverage. People who lose jobs or change jobs would keep coverage automatically.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone, especially the uninsured and underinsured

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. resident would be entitled to comprehensive health coverage, with automatic enrollment at birth or upon establishing residency [S2].

The bill prohibits deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments for covered services, the only exception being prescription drug cost-sharing capped at $200 per year and waived for low-income households [S2].

Covered benefits would include services many current plans lack or limit: dental, vision, and hearing; mental health and substance use treatment; home and community-based long-term care; comprehensive reproductive care including abortion; and gender-affirming care [S2].
HHS would negotiate prescription drug prices and establish a national formulary, replacing the current system in which drug makers set prices for insurers [S2].

During the four-year transition, Medicare would be improved (dental and vision coverage, an end to the 24-month waiting period for people with disabilities) and the Medicare eligibility age would be lowered, with a temporary buy-in plan [S3].
People could see any participating provider — no networks, no out-of-network charges, no balance billing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance companies, whose core business would be phased out (they could sell only supplemental coverage); brand-name drug makers, who would face government-negotiated prices; hospitals and large employers, who would shift from the current mix of private payments to a single government payment system; and taxpayers generally, who would fund the program through a new federal trust fund whose revenue sources are not spelled out in the bill text provided.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, drug makers, hospitals, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate the coverage people have today — employer plans, ACA marketplace plans, and most private insurance — and make it unlawful to sell duplicative coverage, a four-year disruption for people who like their current plans [S2].

It creates a Medicare for All Trust Fund to pay for the program, but the bill text provided does not specify the tax or revenue changes needed to fill it, leaving the largest question — who pays how much — to future legislation [S3].

A single government payer would decide what is covered through national coverage determinations and a national formulary, making HHS the single point of decision for contested or experimental care, with an appeals process but no competing insurers to appeal to [S3].

Hospitals would be paid fixed global budgets rather than per-service fees, and provider payments would be set below current rates in many cases, which could strain hospitals' finances and requires managing insurer-industry job losses with a modest temporary worker-assistance program (at least 1 percent of the budget for up to five years) [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and concrete: universal coverage, no out-of-pocket charges for covered care, and benefits many plans now exclude. The costs are equally real: a once-in-a-generation restructuring of a sector that is roughly a fifth of the economy, elimination of coverage arrangements tens of millions of Americans use today, provider payment cuts that hospitals would resist, and a financing plan the bill does not itself complete. How well it worked would depend heavily on details this bill leaves to HHS and to later Congresses.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read once in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the two-year Congress ended, so it never came to a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the Medicare for All Act on May 17, 2023, with 14 Democratic senators as cosponsors [S1].
That same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S5].
The action history shows no further steps — no hearings, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

In the previous Congress and in this one, similar single-payer bills have been introduced in every Congress for years and have also died without committee action, while the underlying health system was left unchanged [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, brand-name drug makers, and the hospital and employer groups whose role in paying for health care the bill would have replaced — the system they operate was left fully intact for another Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sanders, none of the Senate's 49 Republicans signed on — and even within the Democratic majority, only about a quarter of the caucus sponsored it, with the Democratic chair and floor leader never acting on it.

industries.note: The bill would phase out private health insurance as the main way Americans pay for care — selling coverage duplicating the government plan would be unlawful, and insurers could offer only supplemental benefits. Industry revenue built on employer and marketplace plans would disappear, which is why the industry's interest runs squarely against the bill's benefit to patients.

HHS would negotiate drug prices and run a national formulary, ending the industry's ability to set prices against fragmented private payers. Patients would pay at most $200 a year in drug cost-sharing.

Hospitals would lose bad debt and uncompensated care but be paid through fixed global budgets with caps on executive compensation and restrictions on insurer-style financial arrangements — a large pay cut relative to current private reimbursement rates for many systems.

Employers would stop paying a large share of workers' health premiums (a genuine cost saving) but would also lose the job-based health benefit that ties employees to their jobs and shapes compensation. They could offer only supplemental benefits.
